details: Iodine-131 in nuclear medicine (therapeutic): CHEMICAL FORM: sodium iodide (NaI) solution for oral administration; THERAPEUTIC APPLICATIONS: (1) Thyroid cancer ablation: dose 3,700-7,400 MBq (100-200 mCi); thyroid remnant after surgery; I-131 concentrates in remnant + metastases (NIS symporter); ablative dose to remnant: 50,000-300,000 Gy (total destruction); systemic dose: 5-15 mSv whole body (primarily from blood-borne I-131); (2) Hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease): dose 370-555 MBq; subtotal thyroid ablation; (3) Differentiated thyroid cancer follow-up dosimetry: diagnostic 111 MBq + therapy 3,700 MBq; MECHANISM: I-131 β⁻ (Emax=606 keV; Emean=180 keV) → locally absorbed in thyroid tissue (path length ~2mm in tissue); gamma 364 keV → allows imaging while treating; RELEVANCE TO CHERNOBYL THYROID CANCER: all 6,000+ Chernobyl-attributable thyroid cancer patients received/will receive I-131 therapy as part of standard treatment; ~75% require post-surgical I-131 ablation; dose: 3,700 MBq (100 mCi) standard; SIDE EFFECTS: transient sialadenitis (salivary gland inflammation); radiation gastritis (small dose to GI from swallowed saliva); second primary salivary gland cancer: very small excess (ERR ~0.6/Gy; dose ~0.3 Gy = ERR 0.18 = 18% above background = very small absolute risk)
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl thyroid cancer treatment with I-131: ~75% of 6,000 cases received I-131 ablation; institutional I-131 availability in 1990s Ukraine/Belarus: initially very limited (post-Soviet collapse = supply chain disruption); international medical aid: WHO + IAEA + individual country donations provided I-131 for Ukraine/Belarus in 1990s; protocol: Ukrainian Clinical Protocol (based on ATA 2009 guidelines + adaptations); thyroid cancer survival in Chernobyl cohort: ~98% at 10yr; comparison to sporadic PTC: essentially identical prognosis; KEY DIFFERENCE from sporadic thyroid cancer: (1) Younger age at diagnosis (children exposed 1986 → diagnosed age 20-40); (2) More likely to have lymph node metastases at diagnosis (higher staging); (3) RET/PTC gene rearrangement molecular signature (radiation fingerprint); treatment same regardless; OVERDIAGNOSIS CONCERN: post-2000 widespread ultrasound → microcarcinomas detected → over-treated with I-131; guideline trend toward active surveillance for microcarcinoma <1cm (avoids unnecessary I-131)

details: Cesium-137 in brachytherapy: HISTORICAL USE: Cs-137 (t½=30yr; 662 keV gamma) was widely used in brachytherapy (internal radiation therapy) for: gynecological cancers (cervical; uterine); prostate; other solid tumors; physical form: Cs-137 chloride in metal-sheathed capsules; DOSE RATE: low dose rate (LDR) brachytherapy: 0.4-2 Gy/hr; treatment duration: 20-80 hours; total dose: 30-60 Gy (tumor); REPLACEMENT: Cs-137 largely replaced by Ir-192 (t½=73.8d) in modern HDR (high dose rate) brachytherapy; reasons: (1) Ir-192 allows HDR delivery (dose in minutes vs days → outpatient); (2) Ir-192 source decommissioning in months (vs 30yr Cs-137); (3) Smaller source size (better dosimetry); CURRENT STATUS: Cs-137 brachytherapy: still in use in some low-income countries (cheaper; longer source life = fewer replacements); being phased out globally; SECURITY CONCERN: Cs-137 brachytherapy sources are Category 2-3 (IAEA) radioactive sources; if stolen = potential dirty bomb material; ~100,000 Cs-137 brachytherapy sources worldwide in clinical use or storage; source tracking critical
chernobyl_application: GOIANIA BRAZIL 1987: abandoned Cs-137 brachytherapy unit removed from derelict radiotherapy clinic → scrap dealer opened unit → Cs-137 chloride distributed → 249 contaminated; 4 deaths from ARS; worst radiological accident from medical source; direct lesson: Cs-137 medical sources require: (1) Strict inventory control; (2) Secure storage; (3) National source registry; (4) Disposal program; (5) IAEA Code of Conduct on Safety of Radioactive Sources (2004); CHERNOBYL CONNECTION: Cs-137 released from Chernobyl (85 PBq) = predominantly as Cs-137 chloride/sulfide aerosol = same chemical form as brachytherapy source; behavior in body (if ingested): behaves like Cs-137 brachytherapy = K-analog; uniform whole-body distribution; Prussian Blue oral treatment (same antidote as internal contamination); brachytherapy dosimetry: same radiological physics as environmental Cs-137 dose assessment

details: Strontium-90/Yttrium-90 in ophthalmologic therapy: Sr-90 (t½=28.8yr) → Y-90 (t½=64hr) in secular equilibrium; Y-90 pure beta emitter Emax=2.28 MeV (highest energy pure beta therapeutic isotope in common use); ophthalmic use: (1) Pterygium treatment (benign growth on eye; surgery + beta irradiation prevents recurrence); dose: 20-30 Gy to surface; (2) Ocular melanoma (small tumors; alternative to Ru-106 plaque); (3) Choroidal hemangioma; PHYSICAL: beta range in tissue: Y-90 2.28 MeV → max range ~11mm in tissue; practical treatment depth: 3-5mm (90% dose absorbed); NO GAMMA → applicator handling safe for physician; DOSE RATE: surface dose rate: 0.05-0.1 Gy/s at applicator face; treatment time: 30-120 seconds; APPLICATOR FORM: plano-convex Sr-90 foil (1-3 cm²) in sealed metal housing; source activity: 370-1850 MBq; CHERNOBYL PARALLEL: Sr-90 in environment concentrates in bone (Ca-analog); ophthalmic use = surface beta emitter; same isotope in two roles: (1) Environmental threat (bone cancer risk if ingested); (2) Therapeutic tool (controlled surface dose to eye)
chernobyl_application: Sr-90 internal contamination treatment: no effective antidote once incorporated in bone; prevention: stable Ca supplements reduce Sr-90 bone uptake (competitive inhibition of Ca-like metabolism); after intake: Sr-90 follows Ca metabolism → bone surface → periosteal cells → radiation dose to bone marrow + osteogenic cells; bone cancer risk: UNSCEAR/ICRP: ERR/Gy bone = 0.3; Chernobyl Sr-90 bone doses: contaminated area residents: 0.1-5 mGy/yr bone dose; 50yr cumulative: 5-250 mGy; small excess bone + leukemia risk expected (undetectable); TECHA RIVER: Sr-90 from Mayak → bone doses 0.1-10 Gy in most exposed → confirmed bone cancer excess (in highest-dose individuals); RED FOREST ground: Sr-90 > 10,000 Bq/L groundwater → if ingested by wildlife: bone dose 1-100 mGy/day → potential osteosarcoma risk in long-lived mammals (wolves; bears) in Red Forest; NOT confirmed in wildlife surveys but biologically plausible

details: Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) in diagnostic nuclear medicine: MOST WIDELY USED radioisotope in nuclear medicine; t½=6.02hr; 140 keV gamma (ideal for gamma camera imaging); production: Mo-99 (t½=66hr) → Tc-99m generator; Mo-99 produced in research reactors (NRU Canada; NRR Netherlands; BR2 Belgium; Safari-1 South Africa); supply chain: weekly Mo-99 production → shipped globally → hospital generators → daily elution → Tc-99m for imaging; ANNUAL USAGE: ~40-50 million procedures/yr globally (2026); organ imaging: bone; lung; cardiac; renal; hepatobiliary; sentinel node; sentinel node biopsy: 10-50 MBq; bone scan: 740-1,100 MBq; cardiac SPECT: 555-1110 MBq; effective dose: 1-10 mSv per scan (diagnostic benefit >> radiation risk); CHERNOBYL PARALLEL: CTBTO monitors Tc-99m generator Xe-131m release (Mo-99 → Tc-99m → Tc-99 → then Mo-99 decay chain also releases Xe-131m from fission heritage); major nuclear medicine centers near CTBTO stations = known 'medical source' of Xe-131m; CTBTO discrimination: Xe-131m alone (no Xe-133; no Xe-135) = medical source (Mo-99 generator) not nuclear explosion
chernobyl_application: CHERNOBYL-SPECIFIC DIAGNOSTIC NUCLEAR MEDICINE: (1) WHOLE BODY SCINTIGRAPHY: Tc-99m bone scan used to screen for bone metastases in thyroid cancer (Chernobyl survivors); approximately 6,000 thyroid cancer patients needing periodic surveillance scans = 6,000 × 1 scan/yr × 740 MBq = 4,440 GBq Tc-99m/yr (small fraction of global supply but concentrated demand in Belarus/Ukraine); (2) I-131 WHOLE BODY SCAN: 111 MBq diagnostic I-131 used to detect residual thyroid tissue pre-therapy; 6,000 patients × periodic scans × 111 MBq = significant Belarus/Ukraine I-131 diagnostic demand; (3) THYROID ULTRASOUND: non-nuclear; primary screening tool; 80 MHz probes; no radiation; detected many of the 6,000 Chernobyl cases; (4) FINE NEEDLE ASPIRATION CYTOLOGY (FNAC): guided by ultrasound; cytopathology to distinguish PTC from benign nodule; gold standard for diagnosis; 6,000 FNAC procedures + histopathology for confirmed Chernobyl thyroid cancer patients

details: Iodine-123 and Iodine-125 in nuclear medicine: IODINE-123: t½=13.2hr; decay: electron capture → Te-123; gamma: 159 keV (86%); IDEAL for diagnostic imaging (short half-life = lower dose; 159 keV = optimal for gamma camera); USES: thyroid imaging (NaI-123 capsule; 7-37 MBq); brain imaging (I-123 IBZM for dopamine receptors); cardiac imaging (I-123 MIBG for neuroendocrine); dose to thyroid per diagnostic scan: 7 MBq × 2.2×10⁻⁶ Sv/Bq (adult) = 15.4 mSv to thyroid; COMPARISON WITH I-131: I-123 preferred for diagnostic thyroid imaging in children (lower dose); I-131 retained for therapy + definitive dosimetry; IODINE-125: t½=59.4d; decay: electron capture → Te-125; X-rays: 27-35 keV (low energy); USES: (1) Prostate brachytherapy: permanent implant seeds; 0.37-0.74 MBq per seed; 80-100 seeds per prostate; LDR therapy over 1 year; (2) Brain tumor brachytherapy (interstitial); (3) In vitro radioimmunoassay (now largely replaced by non-radioactive ELISA); CHERNOBYL: thyroid cancer patients: I-123 diagnostic scan to assess thyroid remnant BEFORE I-131 therapy; I-125 brachytherapy not typically used for Chernobyl thyroid cancer (PTC treated with I-131; not seeds)
chernobyl_application: IODINE ISOTOPE FAMILY SUMMARY (radiation medicine perspective): I-131 (t½=8d; β⁻): THERAPY; I-123 (t½=13hr; EC): DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING; I-125 (t½=60d; EC; low-energy X-ray): BRACHYTHERAPY + LABELING; I-124 (t½=4.2d; β+): PET IMAGING (emerging; quantitative thyroid dosimetry); I-129 (t½=15.7Myr; β⁻; 39 keV γ): ENVIRONMENTAL TRACER (reprocessing discharge indicator; Chernobyl trace indicator); CHERNOBYL ISOTOPE: I-131 (dominant short-term) + I-129 (very long-lived trace); I-131 decayed completely within 80 days of accident; I-129 persists at trace levels in environment (HALF-LIFE 15.7 million years; below health concern but detectable by AMS); I-129 in Ukraine soils: 0.1-1 Bq/kg (from Chernobyl); separating Chernobyl I-129 from reprocessing I-129: impossible without atmospheric transport model

details: Plutonium and Americium in medical/civilian applications: AMERICIUM-241 (Am-241; t½=432yr): civilian applications: (1) SMOKE DETECTORS: ~3.7 kBq Am-241 per ionization smoke detector; alpha emitter ionizes air between plates → detects smoke particles; global production: ~300 million smoke detectors; total Am-241 in smoke detectors globally: ~1,110 TBq; ENVIRONMENTAL RELEASE CONCERN: smoke detector fires → Am-241 volatilized; inhalation risk; Am-241 in CEZ: INCREASING (Pu-241 t½=14.29yr → Am-241 ingrowth; peaks 2058.7 at 82.7 TBq in CEZ); Am-241 is more volatile than Pu in fires → preferentially released in wildfires; PLUTONIUM-238 (t½=87.7yr; α emitter): medical use: cardiac pacemakers (1970s-80s; 100,000 implanted); heat source for pacemaker battery; largely replaced by lithium batteries; some Pu-238 pacemakers still in living patients; disposal challenge: cremation releases Pu-238; PLUTONIUM (general): NO therapeutic medical use; highly radiotoxic; alpha emitter; inhalation = severe lung cancer risk; RTOG = Radiation Therapy Oncology Group: no Pu therapies in any trial
chernobyl_application: CHERNOBYL Pu context: Chernobyl dispersed 12 PBq Pu-239+240+241 into environment; CEZ soil Pu-239: 3.7-100+ kBq/m² near reactor; Am-241 from Pu-241 decay (growing since 1986; peaks 2059); Pu isotope ratios in CEZ: Pu-240/Pu-239 = 0.28 (reactor-grade; vs weapons-grade <0.07); Pu-238/Pu-239+240 = 0.03 (identifies reactor origin); NEUTRON ACTIVATION OF Pu-239: in environment; Pu-239 has neutron absorption cross-section but NO sustained chain reaction possible (dispersed; sub-critical always); ENVIRONMENTAL DETECTION METHODS: Pu in soil: ICP-MS (mass spectrometry) or alpha spectrometry; detection limit: 0.001 Bq/g; Am-241: gamma spectrometry (60 keV gamma); much easier to detect than Pu; Am-241 gamma = indicator of Chernobyl Pu deposition location (Pu produces no easily measurable gamma); Am-241 monitoring = PROXY for Pu location; HEALTH RISK: Pu in CEZ soil: not significantly bioavailable (mineralogical form: oxide + silicate); Pu in CEZ dust: inhalation concern; TLV 0.1 Bq/m³ air; CEZ ambient air: <0.001 Bq/m³ (below TLV)

details: Radiation therapy physics (broader context): EXTERNAL BEAM RADIOTHERAPY: linear accelerator (LINAC): 6-18 MV X-rays; typical treatment course: 2 Gy/fraction × 30 fractions = 60 Gy total; 15-30 fractions over 3-6 weeks; mechanism: DNA DSBs in tumor cells → cell death; tumor cells: impaired repair; normal tissue: intact repair → selective tumor killing; COBALT-60 THERAPY MACHINES (historical; still in use in low-income countries): Co-60 (t½=5.27yr); produced: reactor (Co-59 activation); 1.17 + 1.33 MeV gammas; Theratron machines: activity 100-400 TBq; treatment distance: 80cm; dose rate: 1-3 Gy/min; CHERNOBYL ACTIVATION PRODUCTS: Co-58 (t½=70.9d) + Co-60 produced in RBMK from Co-59 impurities in steel + coolant corrosion products; Co-60 in RBMK activated structural steel: problem for decommissioning (long-lived; requires special waste handling); decommissioning workers: Co-60 gamma exposure; IMRT + VMAT: modern LINAC techniques; conform dose to complex 3D tumor shape; minimize normal tissue dose; ALARA in therapeutic context: maximize tumor dose while minimizing normal tissue; same principles as radiation protection but OPPOSITE goal
chernobyl_application: BRACHYTHERAPY COMPARISON TABLE (Chernobyl-relevant isotopes): Cs-137 (t½=30yr; 662keV): gynecological brachytherapy; declining; Sr-90/Y-90 (t½=28.8yr/64hr; β 2.28MeV): ophthalmic applicator; Ir-192 (t½=73.8d; 380keV avg): HDR brachytherapy; gold standard; I-125 (t½=60d; 27keV): prostate seeds; Ra-226 (t½=1600yr; multiple γ): HISTORICAL; replaced (too long-lived for modern handling); At-211 (t½=7.2hr; α): targeted alpha therapy (emerging; NOT yet clinical standard); Pb-212/Bi-212 (t½=10.6hr/60.6min; α): targeted alpha therapy trial; RADIATION THERAPY DOSE COMPARISON: therapeutic dose to tumor: 60-80 Gy; A-bomb survivors at 1km: ~2 Gy; Chernobyl ARS fatalities: 6-16 Gy whole-body; radiation therapy margin from ARS dose: therapeutic = TARGETED; ARS = whole-body; same dose rate and physics; completely different biological context (targeted vs whole-body; fractionated vs acute; etc.)

details: Hospital No. 6 institutional legacy (2026): ORIGINAL INSTITUTION: Moscow Clinical Hospital No. 6 (attached to Institute of Biophysics); principal ARS treatment facility since 1950s (Soviet nuclear weapons program support); principal physician 1986: Dr. Angelina Guskova (1924-2015; died age 91); her partner Dr. Alexander Baranov (treated all 134 Chernobyl patients); RENAMED: 2006 renamed Burnasyan Federal Medical Biophysical Center (FMBC; in honor of Anatoly Burnasyan; Soviet radiation protection pioneer); CURRENT STATUS 2026: FMBC = continues as principal Russian center for radiation medicine; IAEA REMPAN network member; ~60 ARS-specific beds; conducts: radiation medicine research + training + emergency response + consultation; FMBC ARS protocol (2026 version): expanded from Guskova 1986 protocol; now includes: G-CSF (Neupogen) 5 µg/kg/day starting day 1; romiplostim for thrombocytopenia; stem cell mobilization assessment; modern HLA typing (hours vs days in 1986); digital whole-body counter for internal contamination assessment; UKRAINE EQUIVALENT: Shupyk National Healthcare University; Institute of Nuclear Medicine; State Institution 'National Research Center for Radiation Medicine' (Kyiv); principal Ukrainian center; lost access to ZNPP monitoring during occupation
chernobyl_application: Post-Chernobyl radiation medicine advances attributable to Hospital No. 6/FMBC: (1) BMT indication revision: >8 Gy = multi-organ failure limit (Guskova 1988 finding; changed global protocols); (2) Beta burn management: skin damage combined with ARS = worse prognosis (combined injury paradigm); (3) Biological dosimetry: lymphocyte kinetics as dose estimator refined; (4) Long-term follow-up: Hospital No. 6 published 10yr; 20yr; 30yr follow-up of surviving ARS patients; most survivors living normal lives; some: cataracts (as predicted by ICRP); CVD excess (ERR/Gy=0.47); no dramatic excess morbidity in dose range 1-4 Gy survivors; (5) International radiation medicine network: REMPAN; REAC/TS; FNRBC (French equivalent): all strengthened by Chernobyl experience; 40yr LEGACY: 28 ARS deaths; 106 ARS survivors (many still living in 2026; age ~70-80); Hospital No. 6/FMBC followed all 106 survivors for 40yr; unique medical dataset; still being analyzed for late effects
